# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

```{r}
#| label: p2b-disc-setup
#| include: false
loadNamespace("mlogit")   # so summary.mlogit dispatches (CLAUDE.md note)
p_rank   <- summary(model_2b_exploded_draw_final)$CoefTable["stall_x_wolverhampton", "Pr(>|z|)"]
roi_gain <- sprintf("%+.1f pp", 100 * roi_difference_2b_vs_2a$diff_point)
or_over_disc   <- scales::percent(value_bet_baselines_2b$over_round[1] - 1, accuracy = 1)
place_fair_roi <- value_bet_baselines_2b$model_fair[value_bet_baselines_2b$bet_type == "place"]
fav_tie_pct    <- scales::percent(backtest_favourite_win$n_tie_races /
                                  backtest_favourite_win$n_bets, accuracy = 0.1)
```

The exploded model predicts the top-3 finishing order with skill clearly
above chance, yet on neither ranking metric does it match the market. That is
the same pattern papers 1 and 2a found on the win objective — a model with
genuine signal that the starting price nonetheless out-scores — now repeated
on the ranking objective. The reading carries over unchanged: the market
price aggregates information the pre-race feature set does not contain, and
moving from a win objective to a ranking one does not narrow that gap. Turned
into bets, the same picture holds: priced on the real industry-SP book, the
model's place and each-way strategies are both unprofitable, its disagreements
with the market on the losing side where they can be priced.

The second question applies the ranking-fitted model to the win objective,
and here the result is new to the series. Trained on the finishing order
rather than on the winner alone, the model is a better winner-picker than
paper 2a's model: a paired race-level bootstrap puts the gain at
`r roi_gain`, with a 90% interval that lies above zero — the first
distinguishable improvement across the three papers. The mechanism is
supervision, not specification. Depth-3 explosion turns each race into three
nested choice problems — the winner from the full field, the runner-up from
the rest, the third from what remains — so the same races and the same
functional form are estimated from roughly three times as many contrasts, and
the coefficients come back sharper. Wolverhampton is the clean illustration:
its draw term was too noisy to retain under win supervision (Wald
$p \approx 0.066$) but is estimated sharply under the ranking objective
($p =$ `r sprintf("%.4f", p_rank)`), with the same sign and a similar
magnitude. The reading is the narrow one — the ranking objective estimates
the same draw effect paper 2a saw, sharply enough to retain it — not a new
effect uncovered. None of this makes the model profitable, and the gap to the
market is no smaller; the improvement is over paper 2a, not over the price.

Paper 3 changes the model class. A tree-based learner accommodates
non-linearities and feature interactions directly — among them a horse's
going affinity, which the conditional logit can express only through explicit
interaction terms — without the modeller specifying each one in advance.

The betting results put the headline losses in context. Backing every runner
at SP loses `r scales::percent(backtest_betall_win$roi, accuracy = 0.1)` —
worse than the ~`r or_over_disc` over-round alone, the favourite–longshot bias
making longer-priced horses especially costly — while backing the favourite in
every race returns `r scales::percent(backtest_favourite_win$roi, accuracy = 0.1)`
on `r format(backtest_favourite_win$n_bets, big.mark = ",")` races[^fav-ties];
the win model's `r scales::percent(backtest_naive_2b_win$roi, accuracy = 0.1)`
sits between them, beating indiscriminate betting but short of the trivial
favourite strategy. That the residual is mostly margin rather than
mis-selection shows in the place result: against a zero-margin fair book the
model's place selections return
`r scales::percent(place_fair_roi, accuracy = 0.1)`, close to breakeven.
Against a lower-friction market — a Betfair exchange, ~5% commission versus a
~`r or_over_disc` SP over-round — that structural headwind shrinks sharply,
which motivates the early-market convergence strategy as the natural
live-trading direction: not that the model is already profitable, but that it
is being tested against a margin it cannot currently overcome.

[^fav-ties]: Ties for favourite — the lowest decimal starting price shared by
two or more runners — occur in `r fav_tie_pct` of test races and are broken
here by taking the lower-numbered runner.

Evaluating the exotic markets — the exacta and trifecta — is left to future
work: their real prices are the CSF and Tote-pool dividends, which this paper
does not have.
